segments.text: On July 8, 1941, Fritz Schlieper, commander of the German 45th Infantry Division, signed a report on the fighting for Brest-Litovsk.
By then, the main centers of organized resistance inside the fortress had already been crushed.
The report listed captured weapons, prisoners, and the division’s own losses.
But among its military conclusions was a striking statement:  “An overwhelming assault on a fortress held by a brave defender costs a great deal of blood.”
That was the assessment of the man whose division had stormed the fortress.
What happened behind those walls?
Why did the surprise attack fail to bring the resistance to a quick end?
And what does the familiar claim that Brest Fortress held out for more than a month actually mean?
To understand that, we need to return to the morning of June 22.
At dawn on June 22, 1941, German artillery opened fire on Brest Fortress.
Shells exploded among the barracks and warehouses.
People were killed, fires broke out, and communications and water supplies were disrupted.
The war caught more than just soldiers inside the fortress.
Officers’ families were there too, including women and children.
Units from different formations came under attack at the same time.
There was no unified command of the defense from the very first minutes.
Some commanders were killed.
Others were cut off from their men.
Some servicemen managed to leave the fortress.
Those who remained formed small groups wherever they could find weapons, shelter, and someone willing to take command.
German assault units quickly broke into the fortress.
But getting through the gates was not the same as taking control of the entire complex.
Brest Fortress consisted of several sections, separated by rivers, channels, and defensive earthworks.
At its center stood the Citadel.
Barracks, basements, and inner courtyards became individual defensive positions.
German soldiers could advance, only to discover that someone behind them had started firing again.
Near the Kholm Gate, Regimental Commissar Efim Fomin was organizing the defense.
On the morning of June 22, he organized a counterattack from the gate toward the Red Army club, which had been occupied by German troops.
The battle broke into dozens of smaller fights over individual buildings and passageways.
The defenders used rifles, machine guns, and grenades.
When the two sides came face to face, the fighting turned into hand-to-hand combat.
Under these conditions, larger pockets of resistance gradually began to form.
Inside the Citadel, a combined force operated under Captain Ivan Zubachev and Regimental Commissar Efim Fomin.
At the Kobrin Fortification, Major Pyotr Gavrilov became one of the leaders of the defense.
His name would later become particularly associated with the Eastern Fort.
But even with commanders and headquarters in place, the defenders still had no clear picture of what was happening beyond their positions.
They did not know where Soviet troops were, which roads were still open, or whether help could be expected.
The front was moving east.
Behind the fortress walls, the defenders continued fighting, surrounded by the enemy.
The Bug and Mukhavets rivers surrounded the fortress.
On a map, water was close.
But in battle, the distance to the riverbank was measured in more than meters.
The approaches to the rivers were under enemy fire.
Anyone trying to collect water had to leave cover, reach the water, and somehow make it back while being shot at.
After the water supply system was damaged, thirst became one of the most terrible parts of the siege.
Soldiers at their positions suffered from it.
So did the wounded lying in basements, and the women and children trapped inside.
Smoke and fires made conditions even worse.
People tried to reach the water under cover of darkness.
They used whatever containers they could find.
But even a nighttime trip offered no guarantee of returning alive.
The wounded faced especially desperate conditions.
They needed water, bandages, and medical care.
All of these became increasingly difficult to obtain.
Years later, this part of the defense was given a physical form in the fortress memorial.
A sculpture called “Thirst” depicts a soldier reaching toward the water, holding a helmet in his hand.
People were suffering from dehydration within reach of a river.
It remains one of the most painful details of the defense of Brest Fortress, and one that needs no exaggeration.
With every passing day, holding their positions became harder for the defenders.
Some supplies had been destroyed during the bombardment.
Others were cut off.
The fact that warehouses existed inside the fortress did not mean the defenders could reach them or transport what they needed to their own positions.
People searched for surviving food supplies and collected weapons and ammunition.
There was no reliable supply system connecting the scattered groups.
Conditions could be very different even between neighboring buildings.
The Germans used artillery, flamethrowers, and aircraft.
Fortifications were destroyed, and individual positions became isolated from the others.
By June 26, the main pockets of resistance inside the Citadel had been crushed.
Efim Fomin was captured and executed by the Germans.
Ivan Zubachev was also taken prisoner.
He did not survive the war.
He died in a prison camp in 1944.
At the Kobrin Fortification, the Eastern Fort was still holding out.
Its defenders were fighting under the command of Major Gavrilov.
On June 29, after heavy attacks, including strikes from the air, the Germans captured the fort.
A large proportion of the defenders who remained inside were taken prisoner.
By the end of June, the main organized defense of Brest Fortress had come to an end.
That distinction matters.
It would be misleading to imagine that the same garrison held the entire fortress for more than a month, with a unified headquarters and an unbroken defensive line.
In July, resistance continued through individual soldiers and small groups.
Their situation was very different.
They had to find places to hide, avoid searches, search for water, try to escape, or fight if they were discovered.
The single word “defense” covers several distinct stages, and the very different fates of the people involved.
After the fall of the Eastern Fort, Pyotr Gavrilov managed to avoid immediate capture.
He continued hiding among the fortress structures.
What we know about his final weeks inside the fortress comes mainly from testimony and recollections recorded after the war.
That means the details of those days need to be treated with particular caution.
We cannot reconstruct his every movement or every exchange of gunfire.
Gavrilov’s biography gives July 23, 1941, as the date of his capture.
It was the thirty-second day of the war.
He was taken prisoner, badly wounded and severely weakened by exhaustion.
Gavrilov survived the Nazi prison camps, returned home, and was able to tell the story of what he had experienced.
His story became one of the clearest examples of how the collapse of the major defensive positions did not mean that every defender had immediately disappeared from the fortress.
But it would be too definite to call him the very last soldier to remain among its ruins.
The fates of many others were never fully established.
Now, let us return to Schlieper’s report.
In it, the divisional commander acknowledged the determination of the Soviet soldiers, their infantry training, and their willingness to resist.
He also examined why the initial methods of assault had failed to produce the expected result.
This was an internal military document written by the opposing side.
Its author was explaining the actions of his own division and reviewing the outcome of the operation.
For that reason, each claim in the report needs to be compared with other accounts.
Nevertheless, its recognition of the defenders’ determination is unmistakable.
According to the figures given in the report, the division lost 453 men killed or missing, with another 668 wounded.
These were the figures reported for the fighting around Brest-Litovsk as a whole.
They were not a verified, name-by-name count of casualties suffered exclusively within the fortress walls.
Soviet losses were also enormous.
Thousands of servicemen were killed or taken prisoner.
Some of the defenders managed to escape the encirclement.
Brest Fortress did not stop the main forces of the Wehrmacht from advancing east.
For the people who remained inside, that meant their own troops were getting farther away, while their chances of receiving help grew smaller and smaller.
And yet, under those circumstances, they continued to resist.
Their determination was so evident that even the commander of the division attacking them felt compelled to acknowledge it.
After the war, an inscription was discovered inside the ruined fortress.
Its words would become one of the most famous testimonies of the defense:  “I am dying, but I will not surrender!
Farewell, Motherland.”
Beside those words was a date.
The inscription was found in a barracks building that, before the war, had housed the 132nd Separate Battalion of the NKVD Convoy Troops.
The identity of the person who left those words has never been reliably established.
We do not know how long he had been there, whether he was wounded, or whether he was alone.
The inscription cannot tell us his life story.
It preserves only what he himself wanted to say.
The German general left behind a report on the fighting.
An unknown defender left a few words on a wall.
“I am dying, but I will not surrender!
Farewell, Motherland.”
